title: The Bucket of Blood job and learning to play for singers
summary: He plays piano at the Bucket of Blood, unable to transpose for singers, and says Atlantic City's cabarets were the real school.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: But let me tell you about that. There got to be a place right across from where Eubie Blake and Madison Reid and I worked, called the Bucket of Blood. Now I've got this job in the Bucket of Blood. And this is where, in the wintertime, it

was wintertime, and where they would -- if the bartender let the fire go out in the back, because he was the boss of the whole room. They'd beat him up. See, cause the girls used to come in there to get warm. And I was the pianist there, and I did have a drummer there, and neither one of us could play enough to keep us warm. See what I mean? We couldn't play for singers yet, because I don't know how to play for singers, you know.

Every singer would sing in F or C, or keys like that, and I couldn't change no keys, you know what I mean, there's only just playing, I was only just playing, you see? So this was something the youngsters nowadays don't get this practice, to play, you know what I mean? To learn how to play for singers because you can't get that in a conservatory.

You can't get that. You have to get that from only the practicality. It's just like, like a doctor. He can study for four or five years, he can study for ten years, but he comes out and be an intern and know medicine like it should be, know from the actual meeting with the patient and all like that. And understand the symptoms, because later on -- that comes from, I knew from school, the individual differences of people. And some people, like if they've got a -- pneumonia or something like that, they carry an aroma that a doctor can tell
that they -- that this person -- just what disease. Some of them can tell, may even smell cancer. But see, the different diseases.

But, now, not everybody. Cause this person may have it and one would be so faint that you couldn't see it. Anyhow, in Atlantic City at this time, why, this was the greatest school. Because they had about 15 cabarets in the black belt, see, but most of them were patronized by white people. And this was the real age of the ragtime, you see. But in the east we didn't have the whole full bands, yet. We had maybe three or four pieces, and that's the way it went on, you see. So, I did luck up to this Bucket of Blood job, and I got this Bucket of Blood job. And they called it the Bucket of Blood because, outside of the fighting over the fire with the bartender, there used to be somebody's blood would be spilt on the steps every night, see what I mean? Because they'd drag out somebody or drag in somebody, so that's what it was.
